### Iliad, Schliemann and the Mycenaeans

Jo Marchant wrote in Smithsonian magazine: “In The Iliad, Homer tells of how Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, led a fleet of a thousand ships to besiege the city of Troy. Classical Greeks (and Romans, who traced their heritage to the Trojan hero Aeneas) accepted the stories in The Iliad and The Odyssey as a part of their national histories, but in later centuries scholars insisted that the epic battles fought between the Trojan and Mycenaean kingdoms were nothing more than myth and romantic fantasy. Before the eighth century B.C., archaeologists argued, societies on the Greek mainland were scattered and disorganized. \[Source: Jo Marchant, Smithsonian magazine, January-February 2017\]

“At the end of the 19th century, a German-born businessman named Heinrich Schliemann was determined to prove otherwise. He used clues in Homer’s epic poems to locate the remains of Troy, buried in a hillside at Hissarlik in Turkey. He then turned his attention to the Greek mainland, hoping to find the palace of Agamemnon. Near the ruins of the great walls at Mycenae, in the Argolid Peninsula, Schliemann found a circle of graves containing the remains of 19 men, women and children, all dripping with gold and other riches. He hadn’t found Agamemnon — the graves, nearly 3,500 years old, dated to several centuries before the battles of Troy — but he had unearthed a great, lost civilization, which he called the Mycenaean, after the sovereign city of the powerful mythic king.

### Discovery of the "Mask of Agamemnon"

* * *

![Image 2](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202311/221af0dd1dc571c96b78bba4aa7b7f0cf394213f74fc28d7eca48db6394b84c8.jpg)

Mycenaean ring

Following accounts by Pausanias, a famous 2nd century traveler who described "heroes' graves...in the midst of the meeting place," Schliemann searched for the tombs of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra within the walls of the citadel in ancient Mycenae. In December 1876, Schliemann’s team hit pay dirt, discovering the first of five shaft grave that would eventually yield the richest treasure from the past ever found at that point in time. The graves contained bodies "literally covered with gold and jewels." Each face, distinguishable when unearthed but quickly disintegrated by the air, was covered by a gold mask.

Schliemann believed one the masks was the "mask of Agamemnon." He also found gold diadems, gold and silver statuettes, gold sword handles, precious necklaces and bracelets, stone and gold alabaster vases, goblets of gold and silver, and hundreds of other impressive jewels.

The mask, which is now in the Archaeological Museum in Athens, has been dated to 400 years before the Trojan War. No evidence has turned up that Agamemnon was a real person. As far as we know he was only a fictional character.

### ‘Griffin Warrior’ Grave in Pylos

In 2015, archaeologists digging at Pylos, announced they had discovered the rich grave of a soldier that they dubbed the “Griffin Warrior” after images of griffins found on artifacts found in the grave. The grave was discovered by Jack L. Davis and Sharon R. Stocker, a husband-and-wife team at the University of Cincinnati who have been excavating at Pylos for 25 years. The warrior was found in a very rare shaft grave, 5 feet deep, 4 feet wide and 8 long that was in remarkably good condition aside from a one-ton stone, probably once the lid of the grave, which had fallen in and crushed the wooden coffin beneath it. \[Source: Nicholas Wade, New York Times, October 26, 2015 ^^\]

Nicholas Wade wrote in the New York Times: “He lies with a yard-long bronze sword and a remarkable collection of gold rings, precious jewels and beautifully carved seals. Archaeologists expressed astonishment at the richness of the find and its potential for shedding light on the emergence of the Mycenaean civilization. “Probably not since the 1950s have we found such a rich tomb,” said James C. Wright, the director of the American School of Classical Studies at Athens. Seeing the tomb “was a real highlight of my archaeological career,” said Thomas M. Brogan, the director of the Institute for Aegean Prehistory Study Center for East Crete, noting that “you can count on one hand the number of tombs as wealthy as this one.” ^^

“The warrior was buried around 1500 B.C., next to the site on Pylos on which, many years later, arose the palace of Nestor, a large administrative center that was destroyed in 1180 B.C., about the same time as Homer’s Troy. The coffin has long since decayed, but still remaining are the bones of a man about 30 to 35 years old and lying on his back. Placed to his left were weapons, including a long bronze sword with an ivory hilt clad in gold and a gold-hilted dagger. On his right side were four gold rings with fine Minoan carvings and some 50 Minoan seal stones carved with imagery of goddesses and bull jumpers. “I was just stunned by the quality of the carving,” Dr. Wright said, noting that the objects “must have come out of the best workshops of the palaces of Crete.” An ivory plaque carved with a griffin, a mythical animal that protected goddesses and kings, lay between the warrior’s legs. The grave contained gold, silver and bronze cups. The warrior seems to have been something of a dandy. Among the objects accompanying him to the netherworld were a bronze mirror with an ivory handle and six ivory combs. ^^

“Because of the griffins depicted in the grave, Dr. Davis and Dr. Stocker refer to the man informally as the “griffin warrior.” He was certainly a prominent leader in his community, they say, maybe the pre-eminent one. The palace at Pylos had a king or “wanax,” a title mentioned in the Linear B tablets, but it’s not known if this position existed in the griffin warrior’s society. Ancient Greek graves can be dated by their pottery, but the griffin warrior’s grave had none: His vessels are made of silver or gold, not humble clay. From shards found above and below the grave, however, Dr. Davis believes it was dug in the period known as Late Helladic II, a pottery-related chronology that corresponds to 1600 B.C. to 1400 B.C., in the view of some authorities, or 1550 B.C. to 1420 B.C., in the view of others.” ^^

“Archaeologists are looking forward to studying a major unlooted tomb with modern techniques like DNA analysis, which may shed light on the warrior’s origin. DNA, if extractable from the warrior’s teeth, may tell where in Greece he was born. Suitable plant material, if found in the tomb, could yield a radiocarbon date for the burial.” ^^

### Griffin Warrior Burial

* * *

[![Image 3](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202409/a5a8f12d19759283.jpg)](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202409/large-a5a8f12d19759283.jpg)

Griffin Warrior burial

The Griffin Warrior’s grave is a rare undisturbed Mycenaean tomb. Stocker is still amazed at the team’s luck. Not only had the grave escaped the tomb robbers’ notice, if it had been situated just a few feet in any direction, the roots of an olive tree would have penetrated and disturbed it. \[Source: Andrew Curry, Archaeology magazine, September-October 2019\]

Jo Marchant wrote in Smithsonian magazine: “Unlike ancient graves at Mycenae and elsewhere, however, which held artifacts from different individuals and time periods, the Pylos grave is an undisturbed single burial. Everything in it belonged to one person, and archaeologists can see precisely how the grave goods were positioned. \[Source: Jo Marchant, Smithsonian magazine, January-February 2017\]

“Significantly, weapons had been placed on the left side of the warrior’s body while rings and seal stones were on the right, suggesting that they were arranged with intent, not simply thrown in. The representational artwork featured on the rings also had direct connections to actual buried objects. “One of the gold rings has a goddess standing on top of a mountain with a staff that seems to be crowned by a horned bull’s head,” says Davis. “We found a bull’s head staff in the grave.” Another ring shows a goddess sitting on a throne, looking at herself in the mirror. “We have a mirror.” Davis and Stocker do not believe that all this is a coincidence. “We think that objects were chosen to interact with the iconography of the rings.”

“At first, the researchers struggled to precisely date his burial. Soil layers are usually dated based on the shifting styles of ceramics; this grave held no pottery at all. But excavations of the grave’s surrounding soil in the summer of 2016 turned up pottery sherds that point to an archaeological period roughly corresponding to 1500-1450 B.C. So the warrior lived at the very end of the shaft grave period, just before construction of the Mycenaean palaces, including Nestor’s.

“Davis and Stocker believe that the tholos tomb at Pylos was still in use at this time. If the warrior was in fact an important figure, perhaps even a leader, why was he buried in a separate shaft grave, and not in the tholos? Stocker wonders whether digging the shaft grave may say something about the manner of the warrior’s death — that it was unexpected — and proved a quicker option than deconstructing and rebuilding the entrance to the tholos. Bennet, on the other hand, speculates that contrasting burial practices in such close proximity may represent separate local family groups vying for supremacy. “It’s part of a power play,” he says. “We have people competing with each other for display.” To him, competition to amass exotic materials and knowledge may have been what drove the social development of Mycenaean ruling elites.

### Griffin Warrior Artifacts

Ángel Carlos Pérez Aguayo wrote in National Geographic History: Around 1,400 objects have been recovered from the grave. Many are being restored for display in the nearby Chora Archaeological Museum. Hundreds of gems including amethyst, jasper, amber, carnelian, and agate have been recovered. Especially intriguing is a braided necklace that shows signs of damage and repair in antiquity. A faience bead hangs from the necklace of Egyptian manufacture. According to archaeologists, it may have been a spoil of war torn from its owner’s neck and subsequently mended before being buried with the warrior. Six silver cups and several bronze containers for dining purposes were also found, as well as several ivory combs and a mirror. \[Source Ángel Carlos Pérez Aguayo, National Geographic History, August 5, 2022\]

These exquisite artifacts are more than just beautiful; they are evidence of Mycenaean interaction with another culture, the Minoans. Many of the artifacts are from Crete, a large island some 100 miles south of Pylos, which was home to the Minoan civilization. Among these items are gold signet rings bearing engravings of ritual scenes that are typically Cretan. Around 50 gems in the burial are also ornamented with common Minoan motifs, such as bulls. More than 50 sealstones, including a carnelian one featuring three bulls, were found in the Griffin Warrior’s tomb.

* * *

[![Image 4](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202409/5f3e67e0e1bea749.jpg)](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202409/large-5f3e67e0e1bea749.jpg)

Combat Agate

Among the artifacts are: 1) a bronze sword with a gold-embroidered pommel; 2) the Pylos Combat Agate, with an image of the flowing-haired victorious warrior holding an identical type of sword; 3) A gold ring depicting a goddess descending from rocky peaks, flanked by two birds alighting on the peaks; and 4) a gold ring, with two female figures, the larger of whom, likely a goddess, sits on a throne and holds a stemmed object thought to be a mirror. A bird with a long, swallow-like tail perches on the throne, and the wavy lines at the top appear to represent the heavens. cord. \[Source: Andrew Curry, Archaeology magazine, September-October 2019\]

There is also a 5) A heavily corroded bronze disk with gold foil decorations (an X-ray of the disk shows a a sun with 16 points) that was likely attached to the warrior’s armor. 6) A bronze mirror with an ivory handle and an ornate ivory comb are among the artifacts from the grave suggesting that the warrior was a man of high status and was concerned with his appearance.

Perhaps the most exceptional piece from the tomb, the so-called Combat Agate reveals the intertwined influences of these ancient cultures. It took roughly a year to clean and preserve the stone once it had been removed from the tomb, but the results were nothing short of amazing. It is considered to be one of the most exquisite hard stone carvings from all antiquity. Measuring slightly more than an inch long, this tiny, semi-precious stone features a finely detailed depiction of a heated clash between two warriors. A fallen comrade lies beneath their feet as one soldier is poised to pierce the neck of his opponent.

### Combat Agate, Seal Stones and Carved Rings from the Grave of the Griffin Warrior

Andrew Curry wrote in Archaeology magazine: One notable category of objects buried with the Griffin Warrior is seal stones — some 50 of them, made of semiprecious materials. The seal stones, originally used by the Minoans for administrative purposes, are miniature works of art, intricately decorated beyond any functional necessity. In fact, after the stones were cleaned and restored, Stocker’s colleagues made impressions of their designs in putty and found that some of the detail is too small to see with the naked eye, even in the imprints. Many of the stones had been placed on the warrior’s right side, some probably worn as part of bracelets, and others gathered in a bag or pouch that decayed long ago. \[Source: Andrew Curry, Archaeology magazine, September-October 2019\]

The most spectacular seal stone, dubbed the Pylos Combat Agate, is just 1.4 inches wide. Davis and Stocker believe that the artist who created this seal stone was Cretan, because there is, thus far at least, no evidence that artisans on the mainland possessed the skill required to create such an object. The stone depicts a leaping warrior stabbing an armored, spear-wielding foe, while another lies dead at his feet. The scene, like those on many of the other seal stones, is echoed by artifacts found in the warrior’s grave, such as the weapons and scepter laid on his left side. “The sword the victor is using is the same as the sword the warrior is buried with,” Davis says. Six ivory combs and a mirror in the grave suggest the warrior was concerned with his grooming, and perhaps had flowing locks similar to those of the stone’s triumphant warrior. Like the agate’s hero, the Griffin Warrior wore a gold necklace. There is also a nearly microscopic seal stone, less than two-hundredths of an inch across, depicted on a bracelet on the warrior’s wrist. The seal stones in the grave were drilled through, as though to accommodate just such a bracelet cord.

* * *

[![Image 5](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202409/15d7274b5da4d3d5.jpg)](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202409/large-15d7274b5da4d3d5.jpg)

Gold rings from the Griffin Warrior tomb

The sheer number of carved rings and seal stones reinforces the idea that there was something more than mimicry going on. Archaeologist Jan Driessen says seal stones such as those found in the Griffin Warrior’s tomb were highly individual objects that were used by the Minoans for bureaucratic functions, such as to signal identity on official documents. A Minoan would have had one ring or seal stone, or maybe two — but not 50. “It doesn’t make sense to have fifty seal stones,” Driessen says. “The Griffin Warrior was showing off, or maybe the ones who buried him were showing off. There’s obviously Minoan influence, but I do think some of these objects were not used in the same way the Minoans used them.”

“Other objects, too, seem like conscious references to one another. One of four gold rings in the grave shows a Minoan-style bull leaper, echoing a bull’s head once mounted atop a scepter buried nearby. On one seal stone a sun with 16 rays hangs in the sky above two otherworldly creatures with insect-like features, known to scholars of Minoan art as genii. Recent X-rays of a badly corroded bronze breastplate found on the warrior’s legs show that the same 16-pointed star once adorned his suit of armor. “There’s so much evidence that suggests that the Mycenaeans understood Minoan ritual concepts of power,” Davis says. “It seems to us likely that some beliefs originating in Crete had been transplanted intact to Pylos, if not by Minoan missionaries, by converted mainlanders.”

### ‘Griffin Warrior’ and Links Between the Mycenaeans and Minoans

The Griffin Warrior’s grave has offered clues as to how Minoan culture was passed on to the Mycenaeans. Nicholas Wade wrote in the New York Times: He died before the palaces began to be built, and his grave is full of artifacts made in Crete. This is a transformative moment in the Bronze Age,” Dr. Brogan said. The griffin warrior, whose grave objects are culturally Minoan but whose place of burial is Mycenaean, lies at the center of this cultural transfer. The palace of Pylos had yet to arise, and he could have been part of the cultural transition that made it possible.... It is not yet clear whether the objects in the griffin warrior’s tomb were significant in his own culture or just plunder. “I think these objects were not just loot but had a meaning already for the guy buried in this grave,” Dr. Davis said. “This is the critical period when religious ideas were being transferred from Crete to the mainland.” \[Source: Nicholas Wade, New York Times, October 26, 2015 ^^\]

“The grave, in Dr. Wright’s view, lies “at the date at the heart of the relationship of the mainland culture to the higher culture of Crete” and will help scholars understand how the state cultures that developed in Crete were adopted into what became the Mycenaean palace culture on the mainland. Warriors probably competed for status as stratified societies formed on the mainland. This developing warrior society liked to show off its power through high-quality goods, like Cretan seal stones and gold cups — “lots of bling,” as Dr. Wright put it. “Perhaps we can theorize that this site was that of a rising chiefdom,” he said.” ^^

Andrew Curry wrote in Archaeology magazine: “The Griffin Warrior’s grave and its contents are once again changing interpretations of the relationship between the Minoans and Mycenaeans. Much of this has been made possible by the fact that he was buried alone, and that his tomb was discovered undisturbed. This has allowed the team to both study the objects themselves and show how they were originally positioned. Among the thousands of artifacts from the Griffin Warrior’s grave are Minoan-style seal stones of amethyst, carnelian, and agate. Other objects are harder to place, including a sword whose hilt is decorated with tiny gold staples, giving it an embroidered effect, and a boar-tusk helmet, a style of armor that Odysseus wears in Book 10 of the Iliad and that is found on both Crete and the mainland. \[Source: Andrew Curry, Archaeology magazine, September-October 2019\]

“Stocker and Davis have spent the last several years building a case that the Griffin Warrior, and the people who buried him, were not just avid collectors of Minoan art but were also highly clued in to its symbolism. “The Griffin Warrior is saying, ‘I’m part of that Minoan world,’” Stocker explains. “There’s a story we can get at with this burial that we haven’t been able to before.” Scholars agree that the grave is more than a random collection of Mycenaean and Minoan objects. “Here, Cretan art is being reused and repurposed in a local context,” says Nakassis. “That tells us there was a strong connection between people living in Pylos and Crete, a highly informed network of goods, and probably of people, across the Aegean. These weren’t unsophisticated rubes who didn’t understand the beauty and grace of the art they were burying.” Instead, they were deliberately creating a reflection of their worldview.

“Driessen suggests that the idea of classifying art and artifacts as “Minoan” or “Mycenaean” at this time of cross-cultural ferment may not fully reflect the period’s complexity. For example, he believes that mainlanders might have carved the seal stones themselves, having learned from Minoan artisans, or Cretan artisans may have emigrated to the mainland, bringing familiar iconography to new audiences. The connections between the iconography and artifacts have convinced Stocker and Davis that the Griffin Warrior was an informed consumer of Minoan-style objects, not an indiscriminate looter. Somehow, Stocker says, the Griffin Warrior functions as a kind of bridge between the Minoans and Mycenaeans that provides evidence of just how closely interconnected they were. “There’s symbolic unity among the artifacts. We have things that match, assembled with intentionality,” she says. “It’s not randomly accumulated loot. It reflects a story that’s been purposely acquired.”

* * *

![Image 6](https://europe.factsanddetails.com/archives/001/202311/92723cb5b8d6a0d1cbf8aa97b308afea61c1d38381965ce03ed74e0def25ffd7.png)

Mycenaean palace

* * *

### Archaeologist Claims He's Found the Mythical, Homeric Mycenaean Throne

In 2016, Greek archaeologist Christofilis Maggidis claimed that a stone he found was part of the lost royal throne of the rulers of Mycenae, mentioned in both ancient myth and the story of the Trojan War. Maggidis, who heads excavations at the palace of Mycenae site in southern Greece, said that the chunk of worked limestone was found two years ago, in a streambed under the imposing citadel. \[Source: Nicholas Paphitis, Associated Press, June 14, 2016\]

Nicholas Paphitis of Associated Press reported: “He told a press conference in Athens that the royal throne was among sections of the hilltop palace that collapsed during an earthquake around 1200 B.C. Greek Culture Ministry officials have distanced themselves from the identification, citing a separate study that ruled the chunk to be part of a stone basin. But Maggidis said the find was unmistakably made for sitting on, and would have been no use for holding liquids as it is made of porous stone. “In our opinion, this is one of the most emblematic and significant finds from the Mycenaean era," he said. No other thrones have been found in mainland Greece's Mycenaean palaces. An older, smaller example was found in the Minoan palace of Knossos, on the island of Crete. Maggidis said other parts of the throne may lie be beneath Mycenae, and hopes to secure a permit to fully excavate the streambed. The precise type of stone used has not been found anywhere else in the palace of Mycenae, although a similar material was used extensively in the citadel's massive defensive walls and in the magnificent beehive tombs where its rulers were buried.

Image Sources: Wikimedia Commons and Griffin Warrior Tomb website [griffinwarrior.org](https://griffinwarrior.org/griffin-warrior-tomb/)

1 Furniture as an Institution ----------------------------- Empirically, we are all aware that embodied artifacts, such as garments, jewelry and, of course, seating furniture acquires signification according to complex entangled relationships between bodies and the entire artifactual and praxeological environment around them: what exists around the body, and how the body responds to it. The point can be easily made when observing facts that surround us in the modern world: two friends chatting in the cafeteria, attending an archaeological conference or a king enthroned**\[1\]** may all involve similar postures, but the milieu of semantic connections across these examples makes them so distinct as to be virtually incomparable. We may begin by making a point that may be to some counter-intuitive. A ‘logical’ assumption about furniture is that it aims at ‘comfort’. However, this apparent truism may not always stand to scrutiny. Besides the culture-specific connotations inherent in the concept, human anatomical comfort – even if broadly defined as a condition minimizing fatigue and physical stress – rests on accommodation of our S-shaped standing spine and support of our limbs, as well as on _changing_ our posture periodically (chairs: [Cappetti and Di Manso 2021](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_013 "Cappetti, Nicola, and Emmanuel Di Manso. 2021. “Study of the Relationships between Articular Moments, Comfort and Human Posture on a Chair.” Work 68: S59–S68. https://doi.org/10.3233/WOR-208006.Search in Google Scholar"); [Zemp et al. 2015](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_086 "Zemp, Roland, Taylor, William R., and Lorenzetti, Silvio (2015). Are Pressure Measurements Effective in the Assessment of Office Chair Comfort/Discomfort? A Review. Chairs, as well as footstools, that will be our focus here, are parts of a _statement’s material articulation_, whose purpose is accomplished through a culturally implicit dialogue with individuals seated _on_ them. Such artifacts, it can be argued, were important parts of specific statements concerning _human (self-)presentation_, as much related to the human body as dress, jewelry and all other manners of episomatic (-on-the-body) ornamentation, a concept that might be extended to include elaborate coiffures, head ornaments, as well as artefacts born in hand. The purpose of this paper is to explore the content of such cultural statements conveyed through furniture as experienced in a specific sociopolitical context, that of the Mycenaean palatial world, encompassing Crete and various regions of the Greek Mainland c. 1400–1200 BC. 2 Aegean Seats: Finds --------------------- Extant examples of elaborate Aegean Late Bronze Age seats form a small but intriguing corpus. The best known example is, of course, the gypsum seat from the ‘Throne Room’ at Knossos, whose back is attached to the Room’s north wall whose painted decoration presents it as flanked by red palm-trees and reclining wingless griffins. The inventory was made of objects clearly associated with practices revolving around this central core of the _te-ke_ action that took place in a specific occasion. These tablets record, with a remarkable array of descriptive adjectives and other modifications in dative or instrumental forms: vessels (perhaps mostly metal, including jars and tripod cauldrons), ceremonial utensils (including weapons that may be sacrificial implements), and, last but certainly not least, furniture: tables, chairs and stools or footstools. Mycenaean Greek /thornos/ meant ‘chair’ rather than the single ‘throne’ as the seat of the ruler, as the number of /thornoi/ recorded in these tablets (five or six) indicates. The term did not have the precise associations to the office of kingship of later Greek θρόνος. The latter exclusive meaning of θρόνος as a specifically royal seat is not yet developed in Homer, while the earliest secure attestations of θρόνος as a metonymic reference to royal power occur in Pindar and the Attic tragic poetry in the 5th century BCE ([Petrakis 2020a](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_045 "Petrakis, Vassilis. 2020a. “Mycenaean thórnoi, Homeric θρόνοι: Textual Perspectives”. On this record, which is not related to the **Ta** set and certainly attributed to a different ‘scribe’, wooden parts of either a building or a ship are listed, thereby providing the context in which the interpretation of _ta-ra-nu_ as a permanent structural component may appear preferable. The relative ambiguity of the term is also followed on the use of the corresponding epic Ionic type θρῆνυς: to indicate the meaning of ‘footstool’ the epic tradition utilized the phrase θρῆνυς ποσὶν “a θρῆνυς _for the feet_” consistently located under the elaborate seat (_Iliad_ 18.390; _Odyssey_ 1.131, 4.136, 10.315, 10.367). Such modification of θρῆνυς indicates that the term could be a support for other things too; from that perspective, it is possible to view ποσὶν as added for disambiguation (although, of course, the formulaic nature and metrical constraints of Homeric verse-making must be also taken into account). In the case of the **Ta** set, the interpretation of _ta-ra-nu_ as either a ‘stool’ or a ‘footstool’ is ensured by its association with _to-no_, but identifying the exact meaning is not straightforward. If we view the **Ta** set as including the authentic notes made by a palace official entrusted with the meticulous recording of items associated with a specific ceremonial occasion, it is important to underscore the following features of the seating furniture entries in the **Ta** set: 1. six out of the thirteen records concern either chairs or associated furniture (stools or footstools, which are indicated by _ta-ra-nu-we_) 2. the descriptive vocabulary concerning those items is the most elaborate attested amongst the entries. It is worth noting that two _ta-ra-nu-we_ from the Pylos **Ta** set, likely footstools, bear inlaid figural decoration _including human figures_: _a-ja-me-no_, _e-re-pa-te-jo_, _a-di-ri-ja-pi_, _re-wo-pi-qe_ /aiaiménos elephantéiois andriámphi léwomphi-kwe/ “inlaid with ivory men and lions” (**PY Ta 708**.2B); _a-ja-me-no_, _e-re-pa-te-jo_, _a-to-ro-qo_, _i-qo-qe_, _po-ru-po-de-qe_, _po-ni-ke-qe_ /aiaiménos elephantéiō anthrṓkwō íkwō-kwe pōlupódē-kwe phoiníkē-kwe/ “inlaid with an ivory man (or: human?) and a horse and an octopus (or nautilus?) and a palm-tree(?)” (**PY Ta 722**.1). Although helmets are not explicitly mentioned in the context of footstool decoration,**\[4\]** the above descriptions show that the figural decoration on the Archanes footstool may not have been an isolated case. Considering the explicit textual and archaeological evidence for footstool decoration, it is not unlikely that other fragments of figural or non-figural inlaid decoration, which are known from Knossos (“Tomb of the Tripod Hearth” in Zapher Papoura), Mycenae (“Aegisthus” tholos tomb; chamber tomb 27), Prosymna (chamber tomb II), Pylos (tholos tomb III in Kato Englianos) and Thebes (Kordatzis plot) (see [Petrakis 2022](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_047 "Petrakis, Vassilis. 2022. “Πάντας τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ: Συμβολικές εκφράσεις στα μυκηναϊκά υποπόδια.” In The Ancient Throne: The Mediterranean, Near East, and Beyond from the 3rd Millennium BCE to the 14th Century CE. These further possible examples seem to date within the 14th and 13th centuries BCE. The possibility that some of these inlaid ivories may represent parts of the decoration of footstools similar to the one from Archanes, although often deemed impossible to confirm due to the fragmentary state of the pertinent ivory finds,**\[5\]** can be further explored, especially as such inlaid motifs have a significantly broad geographic distribution. Even the less common type, the helmeted head, is found in rich assemblages in the Greek Mainland (Mycenae in the Argolid and Spata in east Attica), Crete (Archanes in north-central Crete part and Chania and Phylaki Apokoronou in west Crete), as well as occasionally outside the Aegean (Enkomi on Cyprus, Mitza Purdia di Decimoputzu in Sardinia). The important implication is that the Archanes find may not be truly exceptional, but rather an _exceptionally preserved_ example of decoration that may well have been more common among footstools during the 14th and 13th centuries BC, when such ivory motifs occur, albeit in conditions that do not presently allow confident reconstruction of their original arrangement. 4 Learning to ‘Read’ Decorated Objects with Some Egyptian Help -------------------------------------------------------------- The ‘loaded’ significance of seated posture in ceremonial contexts, as strongly suggested by the evidence of the Pylos **Ta** tablets, makes it worthy to explore the possibility that the imagery on these artifacts, especially the figural motifs on the footstools was strategically _chosen_ to convey specific statements related to the seated posture. For this purpose, illuminating parallels can be sought, which may provide us with examples of the range of possibilities offered by such a use of furniture decoration. We must note from the outset that the employment of symbolic decoration on furniture is broadly attested, and manifest itself in interesting cross-cultural homologies. The seated posture as a metaphor of domination, as well as a reference to the status of senile age, as well as, to quote Galen Cranz once more, quite loaded “ideas about comfort”. It is perhaps in this light that we must examine specific broad trends, including the zoomorphic depiction of specific furniture parts, ranging from the well-known image of the 6th millennium BCE Çatalhöyük “goddess” whose arms rest on felines (or could they be feline-shaped armrests?) to the “legs” of furniture alluding to bovid or feline forms (attested in Egypt and Mesopotamia). Alluding to the form of a powerful animal (a bull, a leopard or a lion), use of the furniture becomes a semantic assemblage with an artifactual and a live human component. Human furniture-users dominate or co-operate with the crafted item as they interact with it, as they sit, eat or sleep on it; this condition, in turn, might be taken to allude to dominion over the animal whose figure the crafted item has borrowed ([Petrakis and Petridis 2022](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_048 "Petrakis, Vassilis, and Platon Petridis. 2022. “The Public Setting”. Despite the fundamental differences between Egyptian and Aegean iconography, especially regarding the representation of ‘foreigners’ (arguably _absent_ from the Aegean repertoires, with a few rare exceptions, see [Blakolmer 2012](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_010 "Blakolmer, Fritz. 2012. “The Missing ‘Barbarians’: Some Thoughts on Ethnicity and Identity in Aegean Bronze Age Iconography.” Talanta 44: 53–77.Search in Google Scholar")), in both cases, such concepts and categories as “magic”, “cosmology”, “political propaganda” and “diplomacy”, that _we_, from our _etic_ perspective, consider separate, were seamlessly interwoven. The frequent verbal expression whereby vassal rulers refer to themselves as the “footstools” of the Egyptian ruler is also found in the contemporary diplomatic correspondence on the Tell El Amarna tablets. Inferior rulers such as Rib-Haddi of Byblos or Biryazawa of Damascus are self-represented (or so it seems from our extant documentation) as “footstools at the feet” (GI\]Š.GIR.GUB GIR.MEŠ-_ka_) of the king (EA 84.4; 106.6–7; 195.9–10; 241.7**\[6\]**), in terms that have justifiably been viewed as “self-humiliatory” ([Mynárová 2007](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_037 "Mynárová, Jana. 2007. Language of Amarna, Language of Diplomacy. Perspectives on the Amarna Letters. Prague: Czech Institute of Egyptology.Search in Google Scholar"): 131–146). The same metaphor is also well known from the Old Testament where the “footstool” is a common metaphor for one’s enemies or subordination (e.g. _Isaiah_ 66:1; _Psalms_ 110:1). It would not be an overstatement to observe that such expressions are verbal equivalences of the figural decoration of Egyptian “ceremonial” footstools. The iconographic and textual evidence discussed above has the potential to refresh considerably our perspective on the Archanes footstool and possibly similar examples from the Aegean. The helmeted heads and figure-of-eight shields on the Archanes footstool allow, viewed in the side light afforded by the Egyptian evidence, interesting insights. It is important us keep in mind throughout that the figural decoration of these items were components of a specific visual intent: their _display_ purposes were only accomplished with the feet of specific human agents _on_ them. Our discussion of the Egyptian footstools (and pertinent textual references) has gathered enough momentum to make the suggestion that the intended _use_ of the Archanes (or a similar) footstool might convey the message of trampling helmeted heads and figure-of-eight shields ([Petrakis 2022](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_047 "Petrakis, Vassilis. 2022. “Πάντας τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ: Συμβολικές εκφράσεις στα μυκηναϊκά υποπόδια.” In The Ancient Throne: The Mediterranean, Near East, and Beyond from the 3rd Millennium BCE to the 14th Century CE. The depiction of such motifs in isolation, without explicit references to their _military use_, lends strong support to their interpretation as apotropaic images, in a function that is, of course, ultimately derivative of their original use in combat. It can be questioned whether a distinction between, on the one hand, the various shades of “magical” functions (including amuletic or apotropaic, aimed at guarding off evil and all kinds misfortune) and, on the other hand, “power display” (aimed at generating a politically loaded impression to the viewer) is emically meaningful when one discusses the imagery of an item such as the Archanes footstool. It is not impossible that, specifically in their employment for the decoration of such a prestigious item (whose deposition as a grave-good must be viewed within the well-documented conspicuous consumption strategies evident in Late Bronze Age Aegean mortuary practices), the two categories are conflated. The argument for such an apotropaic use of defensive military equipment need _not_ presuppose the adoption of beliefs or practices from non-Aegean sources (as in [Davaras 2022](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_020 "Davaras, Costis. 2022. “Possible Origins and Meaning of the Minoan Figure-of-Eight Shield.” In Kleronomia: Legacy and Inheritance. Studies on the Aegean Bronze Age in Honor of Jeffrey S. Soles, edited by Joanne M. A. Murphy, and Jerolyn E. Morrison, Prehistory Monographs 61, 125–36. Philadelphia: INSTAP Academic Press.10.2307/j.ctv13nb6xx.19Search in Google Scholar"): 131–133). Shields and helmets were invented to protect their carriers in combat; it is certainly equally plausible (and more economical) to assume that their apotropaic signification may have been independently developed in various cultural contexts – at least so in the absence of compelling evidence suggesting otherwise. It is reasonable to argue that, as is common with apotropaic imagery, the magical defense of the shield served to protect the object it adorned and/or the human agents associated with it. These may include the users or occupants of a building adorned with wall-paintings of such imagery, or the bodies adorned with jewelry or other “personal” items _worn_ on the body (most prominently seals and signet-rings). However, such use seems to run counter to the signification of motifs used on footstools, items which would be physically _trampled_ by the user of the object. In order to better assess the significance of this condition, it might be worth looking _into how the objects depicted (shield and helmet) were used_. For this we must return to authentic emic sources, namely the iconographic statements produced within the same cultural context as the isolated images. Although quite few, such representations have been a continuous focus of research (and, perhaps understandably, very popular modern choices of illustration), obscuring, as Rehak (1999: 234) once noted, the overall symbolic function of such militaristic motifs. However, a point can be made that at least some of these combat scenes, although seemingly distinct from the occurrence of figure-of-eight shields and helmets as ‘isolated’ (so arguably symbolic) motifs, are in fact in good accordance with it. Let us focus on a potentially important observation. On three of these images, the gold cushion and the “Battle in the Glen” ring from Mycenae, as well as the Pylos “Combat Agate”, one notes that it is the (to be) _defeated_ figures that bear the most elaborate defensive gear. Although the ultimate end of the scene is not depicted, the snapshot depicted _clearly_ indicates it: the penetration of a point at the base of the neck is fatal, as any viewer of the image would acknowledge. The composition highlights this specific instance when the outcome is decided. The dead are not depicted, and there are many possibilities as to why this is so: it can be argued that death is clearly implicated, so it could be superfluous and, therefore, carrying less dramatic effect; conceivably, however, considering the overall scarcity of explicit physical violence (e.g. decapitation or mutilation or blood) in Aegean imagery, one might also suggest that the topic might have been inappropriate. At the same time, one may note that deceased warriors can be shown, using a familiar Aegean ‘loose limb’ conventional posture, as in the case of the killed warrior on the Pylos “Combat Agate”. We may find a parallel in the non-visual presentation of onstage violence (especially violent death) in Attic drama, which could nonetheless be verbally presented ([Sommerstein 2004](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_070 "Sommerstein, Alan, H. 2004. “Violence in Greek Drama”. Of course, as in Aegean imagery, killed victims were certainly displayed too on certain occasions, as demonstrated in Aeschylus’ _Agamemnon,_**\[8\]** but the act of killing itself was not part of performed displayed action. The overwhelming figures (which may well be termed “victors”) are all youthful males and carry invariably less gear. The emphasis in their representation is clearly on their physical strength, which is emphasized by explicit indication of muscular anatomy (nowhere else more clear than in the Pylos “Combat Agate”) and their beauty, made explicit by grooming (hair is long and well-tended) and bodily adornment. One particularly notes the necklace and the seal (tied with cord on the wrist of the left hand) of the victor on the Pylos “Combat Agate” ([Stocker and Davis 2017](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_071 "Stocker, Sharon R., and Jack L. As this ‘imbalance’ in military equipment between ‘victor’ and ‘victus’ does not seem an isolated case, but a conscious iconographic choice, distributed enough to be given so different stylistic treatments in the Mycenae and the Pylos seals, it seems legitimate to explore its significance. In this regard, it is noteworthy how the content of the image brings to mind a very popular leitmotiv in popular myths and narratives, which may be outlined as follows: the ‘hero’ (for we may be permitted to call him so), by his _virtue_ alone, his strength, courage, momentum and _often_ with an implicit but all too important divine favor would emerge triumphant over far better equipped opponents, who may even underestimate him. This theme, that of the ‘all-winning outsider’ is very well known from its variants. It is reflected in the adventures of the archetypal hero Herakles, who uses the most primitive weapon conceivable – a piece of wood- which he meaningfully _made it himself_, a point emphasized by various sources, making thus this weapon into an expansion of the hero’s physical virtue.**\[9\]** An exact parallel to Herakles’ club, equally popular, is Samson’s donkey jawbone, another improvised weapon, with which he killed a thousand Philistines (_Judges_ 15:15–16). The hero’s opponents are superior – or _so they seem_. They may possess superhuman strength and qualities that need to be overcome. If they are human, they are numerous and better equipped, such as the Orchomenians led by Erginus or the Philistines. Still, wearing a helmet or carrying your shield cannot stop the hero’s overwhelming power. The outcome of the combat is not related to equipment: the hero wins because of being _who he_ i_s_. Minimally armed, the Aegean hero, exemplified in such representations, appears with a male body at its prime, but still very young, as the beardless face may indicate. He is also groomed to look his best, with long hair flowing in the dynamic movement and, as revealed by the more detailed “Combat Agate” presentation, adorned with a necklace and a seal in his wrist. He only wears boots and codpiece, and the nudity of the torso and limbs facilitates the display of youthful masculinity, energy and vitality. The Aegean hero’s only gear is the long sword, the elite weapon par excellence, whose scepter-like form makes it also an appropriate _insigne dignitatis_. This weapon, and the practical skills involved in its efficient use, acquired through specialized training, is completely different than the primitive club and jawbone employed by folk-heroes, while also constituting an apparent exception to the ‘unarmed victor’ motif. However, the elite connotations of long swords, clear in their contextual associations in rich Early Mycenaean burials, may explain its occurrence as an acceptable exception made to this marker of the victor’s _status_ (cf. also [Kramer-Hajos 2016](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_032 "Kramer-Hajos, Margaretha. 2016. Mycenaean Greece and the Aegean World: Palace and Province in the Late Bronze Age. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.10.1017/CBO9781316227718Search in Google Scholar"): 33–39). We must note that, except from this explicitly offensive, not defensive, weapon, the hero enjoys no protection from helmet, cuirass or shield, because he does not _need_ it – and because the protection he may enjoys can be implicitly divine. We may observe that, although entirely overcome by our ‘hero’, the opponent(s) are not trampled in any known composition. Even when they are down, the hero steps beside or among them ‒ an exception being the “Simile Stele” from Shaft Grave V (the one where a shield-carrying figure is trampled by a chariot). In no way are they humiliated in the same way as the enemies of the Egyptian king are; such imagery, although canonical in Egypt ([Janzen 2013](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_029 "Janzen, Mark D. 2013. Such dominance over helmeted heads and shields then might emerge as carrying an overtly victorious statement: all enemy defenses are crushed; shields and helmets do not protect them; they are subdued. This concerns a possible semantic contradiction between the (apparently benevolent) protective function of the isolated helmet/shield and the physical dominance over them ‒ the latter potentially suggesting their neutralization or annulment. To phrase it in simple terms: how appropriate would it be to trample on a benevolent symbol? In the reconstruction, these triangular pieces are shown to join to produce a pattern of repeated square motifs, in which a dark-light hue contrast is produced. The motif is considered non-figural, but it might be interpreted as the variant of a built ashlar _wall_.**\[10\]** The contrast of hues may, in fact, be considered as alluding to the checkerboard motif, well known as a representation of ashlar built constructions in Aegean iconography ([Blakolmer 2020](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_011 "Blakolmer, Fritz. 2020. “Approaching Ashlar Masonry through Minoan and Mycenaean Iconography: Architectural Functions, Urbanistic Contexts and the Problem of Color and Material.” In Ashlar: Exploring the Materiality of Cut-Stone Masonry in the Eastern Mediterranean Bronze Age, edited by Maud Devolder, and Igor Kreimerman, Aegis 17, 73–96. Louvain-la-Neuve: Presses Universitaires de Louvain.Search in Google Scholar"): 76–78, Figs. 2.5–2.9). If this conjecture is accepted, we may explore the hypothesis that the Mycenae footstool, like the Archanes one, bore decoration alluding to a _protective_ device: strong walls defend a city in the same way that the shield and helmet protect the fighting warrior. It becomes quite tempting to assume that this decoration functioned also along the same symbolic language evident in the Archanes footstool: complete with the user’s feet on it, the footstool would convey the message of crushing the depicted wall, (any) opponent’s defenses. It might not be too far-fetched to suggest that, as with the Archanes assemblage, an attempt was made to make up for the destructive spirit of this bodily statement with the addition of one seal (no exuberance here) bearing an overtly benevolent protective symbol: the _isolated_ boar’s tusk helmet. 6 Participatory Iconography --------------------------- The attempt made here to interpret the decoration of the Archanes footstool was based on the hypothesis that this functioned in a synergy with the bodily _participation_ of the footstool’s user. This can be argued to be a further example – and an even more lucid one- of _participatory_ iconography in the Mycenaean palatial world. The basis of this approach to the iconography of such “throne rooms” is the observation that the composition flanking the “throne” could _only be completed with a living agent being an integral part of it_. This observation may set the perception of this scene within a nexus of performed action (the action of the agent taking their place in the “throne”), as well as with a dynamic statement emanating actively out of the scene and directed specifically to the viewer(s) within a specific temporal frame: a “moment” in which the viewer confronts the composite \[seating agent + decoration\] image, whereby they are “enchanted” or “captivated”. Being extraneous to the process of such performances, we may wonder ‘how do they do it’, but this is a question we cannot comprehensively answer. It is also interesting – and highly relevant to the topic we discuss – how this effect of “captivation” may often be ultimately related with the kind of magical background that is (explicitly or implicitly) considered to govern the _unequal_ relationship between the producer of ‘art’ and the viewer, a background reflected in the modern cultural context by the (often casual) use of the term ‘inspiration’ (cf. [Gell 1998](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_028 "Gell, Alfred. 1998. Let us, however, return to the dichotomy between ‘panoptic’ and ‘participatory’ imagery. Most iconographic representations, especially narrative scenes, might be thought as representing ‘panoptic’ viewpoints, in which the observer is _detached_ with regard to what is depicted. The consumption of a scene on a miniature wall-painting, an inlaid dagger, a seal or signet-ring involves a viewer that is completely extraneous, not implicated at all with whatever action or figure is shown on the image. Bennet has used an interesting term for such a viewer-image relationship: “third-person” ([Bennet 2007](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_007 "Bennet, John. 2007. “Representations of Power in Mycenaean Pylos: Script, Orality, Iconography.” In Στέφανος Αριστείος. Athens: Institute of Historical Research, Department of Greek and Roman Antiquity (ΚΕΡΑ), National Hellenic Research Foundation.Search in Google Scholar")\]: 26). But the iconographic “framing” iconography of the “participatory” type appears to be, as Bennet has most perceptively called it, “_first_ person”: the message is emanating out of the image itself, with part of the imagery being completed by the _seated individual_ itself who, by taking their place on their throne, is being integrated within the pre-set imagery of predators (griffins and/or felines) apparently tamed, yet powerful and protective to the throne’s occupant and the institution they represent. In this way, as [Bennet (2015](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_008 "Bennet, John. 2015. “Telltale Depictions: A Contextual View of Mycenaean Wall-Paintings.” In Mycenaean Wall Painting in Context: New Discoveries, Old Finds Reconsidered, edited by Hariclia Brecoulaki, Jack L. Davis, and Sharon R. Stocker, Μελετήματα 72, 21–34. Athens: Institute of Historical Research, Department of Greek and Roman Antiquity (ΚΕΡΑ), National Hellenic Research Foundation.Search in Google Scholar"): 26) has eloquently phrased it, third-person statements of the type “X is Y and there they are” of panoptic narrative imagery, become “I am Y and here I am”, within captivating performances that were strategically choreographed in the throne rooms of Knossos and in the hearth-dominated palatial _megaron_ of Pylos, and perhaps of Tiryns and Mycenae as well. The interpretation of the _function_ of the decorated Archanes footstool argued so far (cf. also [Petrakis 2022](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_047 "Petrakis, Vassilis. 2022. “Πάντας τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ: Συμβολικές εκφράσεις στα μυκηναϊκά υποπόδια.” In The Ancient Throne: The Mediterranean, Near East, and Beyond from the 3rd Millennium BCE to the 14th Century CE. Proceedings of the Workshop held at the 10th ICAANE in Vienna, April 2016, edited by Liat Naeh, and Dana Brostowsky Gilboa, Oriental and European Archaeology 14, 61–84. Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press.Search in Google Scholar")) may offer a further example of the same kind of first-person statement, generated by a further example of participatory imagery in the Late Bronze Age Aegean. 7 Further Points for Potential Expansion on Aegean Participatory Imagery à Propos Decorated Footstools ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Suggesting that Mycenaean footstools with similar figural decoration had functions analogous to the one proposed here for the Archanes example is able to suggest certain points for potential further exploration of Aegean participatory imagery. 1. Unlike the ‘thrones’ involved in first-person imagery in the Knossos and Mainland ‘Throne Rooms’, the _mobility_ of the footstool enables such participatory imagery to be carried out of the closed (however spacious), architecturally defined, palatial _indoor_ space (which is the only kind of space adorned with wall-paintings in the Bronze Age Aegean). It might be significant to revisit one of the most explicit depictions of a footstool in Aegean art, the one used by the seated figure on the Tiryns ring ([Figure 1](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_fig_001) top left). The footstool there is used in an _outdoor (or, at least, open space)_ setting, as clearly suggested by the depiction of celestial bodies on the upper part of the scene and the depiction of a _folded_ seat – the latter indicating furniture explicitly produced to be _mobilized._ Such flexibility in the use of footstools both in indoor and outdoor settings can suggest their broader and more effective use in elite display strategies. 2. The interpretation of the footstool decoration advanced here generates the anticipation that some _chairs_ (/thornoi/ in Mycenaean Greek) would have been similarly decorated, enhancing the same message when used with footstools. At the very least, the elaborately decorated /thornoi/ in the Pylos **Ta** series, as well as the parallel function of such imagery on footstools as well as chairs in Egypt, are sufficient to leave this possibility open. Although we have so far failed to identify remains of such chairs in mortuary or other contexts, it cannot be excluded that some of the disparate ivory inlaid work with figural decoration might belong to such perishable items. 3. We may examine the question of the _origins_ of such imagery in the Aegean. The Egyptian parallels cited above entered our analysis as analogies aiming to enhance our understanding of Mycenaean footstools and certainly not to imply direct Egyptian or other influence on Mycenaean iconography. Evidence for this is ambiguous. On the one hand, it can be argued that such imagery may be indicative of a _shared_ mentality prevalent among East Mediterranean court lifestyles ([Walsh 2014](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_080 "Walsh, Carl R. 2014. “The High Life: Courtly Etiquette in the Late Bronze Age Eastern Mediterranean.” In Current Research in Egyptology 2013. Proceedings of the 14th Annual Symposium, University of Cambridge, United Kingdom, March 19–22, 2013, edited by Kelly Accetta, Renate Fellinger, Pedro Lourenço Gonçalves, Sarah Musselwhite, and W. Paul van Pelt, 201–16. Oxford/Philadelpheia: Oxbow.10.2307/j.ctvh1dknj.21Search in Google Scholar"), [2016](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_081 "Walsh, Carl R. 2016. The Transmission of Courtly Lifestyles in the Bronze Age Eastern Mediterranean. Unpublished Doctoral Dissertation, University College London.Search in Google Scholar")\]), maintained through a steady flow of gift-exchange that we classify as ‘diplomatic’. However, Aegean elites were peripheral to the East Mediterranean elite cosmopolitanism, as suggested by their absence from the Amarna correspondence (despite the contemporary rise of Mycenaean imports in Egypt and elsewhere), and their seeming exclusion from the club of the ‘Great Kings’ of the time – the latter with the notable exception of some Hittite diplomatic flattery intended in the context of specific, local issues affecting the Hittites but, it seems, not ‘international’ matters. If we interpret correctly the influx of imported items bearing the cartouche of Amenhotep III (or his wife Tiye) around the Aegean alongside the reference of (possibly) Aegean place-names on the well-known Kom El-Hettân inscription ([Cline and Stannish 2011](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_014 "Cline, Εric H., and Steven M. Stannish. 2011. “Sailing the Great Green Sea? Amenhotep III’s ‘Aegean List’ from Kom El-Hetan once More.” Journal of Ancient Egyptian Interconnections 3: 6–16. https://doi.org/10.2458/azu_jaei_v03i2_cline.Search in Google Scholar")), as reflecting a sudden intensification of Egyptian-Aegean relationships at that time, possibly even a diplomatic(?) expedition during this ruler’s reign (so contemporary with Late Minoan/Late Helladic IIIA1), then it becomes attractive to consider that Aegean elites would have been exposed to Egyptian display practices, which were certainly employed by 18th Dynasty rulers, including Amenhotep III himself ([Figure 3](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_fig_003)). An appropriation or adaptation of such practices would not be unthinkable in such a context. The hypothesis of an Egyptian appropriation need not be incompatible with certain clues suggesting that Aegean elites were already well set up to receive such external stimulation. We have certain clues that, although not entirely conclusive, may deserve consideration, as they suggest that footstools and participatory imagery were formed earlier than the alleged Egyptian expedition. We have to evidence for footstools on the Greek Mainland before the Late Bronze Age, while we may also note that the clearest evidence for such furniture dates to the palatial (14th–13th centuries BCE), rather than the Early Mycenaean period (17th–15th centuries BCE). However, the representation of a footstool on a figure from a Middle Minoan IIIA ‘shrine’-model from Galatas ([Rethemiotakis 2010](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_055 "Rethemiotakis, Georgios. 2010. “A Shrine-Model from Galatas”. In Cretan Offerings. Studies in Honour of Peter Warren, edited by Olga Krzyszkowska, BSA Studies 18, 293–302. London: The British School at Athens.Search in Google Scholar")), as well as the possible interpretation of an ivory inlay with relief spiral decoration from the Late Minoan IB palace complex of Kato Zakro (cf. [Poursat 1977a](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_050 "Poursat, Jean-Claude. 1977a. Les Ivoires Mycéniens. Essai sur la Formation d’un Art Mycénien. Bibliothèque des Écoles Françaises d’Athènes et de Rome 230. Athens: École Française d’Athènes.Search in Google Scholar"): 32, no. 6), can suggest the existence of Minoan footstools as early as the 17th century BCE. Without disregarding the possibility of independent invention, the most likely scenario is that Mainland footstools may have a been a cultural borrowing from Crete.**\[11\]** Secondly, a potential example of participatory imagery, the decorative frame of the Knossian gypsum throne – arguably the prototype for the relevant feature in the Mainland _megara_ – was perhaps already in place in Late Minoan II ([Galanakis et al. 2017](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/janeh-2024-0002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOorPnqQut2dFhq-gnyssMwmE_JwJEkPk2Lqi3WpzFNS_QPblKoKo#j_janeh-2024-0002_ref_027 "Galanakis, Yannis, Efi Tsitsa, and Ute Günkel-Maschek. 2017. “The Power of Images: Re-examining the Wall Paintings from the Throne Room at Knossos.” The Annual of the British School at Athens 112: 47–98. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0068245417000065.Search in Google Scholar"): 27–34). The above evidence suggests that, within a context formative for what would become the Mycenaean palatial institutional complex, both components (footstools and the participatory first-person imagery statements) were already present _prior to_ the episode in which _possible_ Egyptian influence would be arguable (the Late Minoan/Late Helladic IIIA1 _hypothetical_ Egyptian royal expedition). Whether the exotic trigger occurred or not, the elements were there, constituting the proper background for the participatory function of footstool decoration. Although the role of Egyptian seeds can be debated, we may highlight the important function of Aegean (and perhaps specifically Knossian) fertilizers in shaping a further innovative use of such imagery. 21.content:
Abstract
--------

In May 2015, a University of Cincinnati team unexpectedly discovered a large stone-built tomb of Late Helladic IIA date near Tholos Tomb IV on the first day of renewed excavations at the Palace of Nestor, Pylos. Hundreds of artifacts of gold, silver, bronze, ivory, and semiprecious stones were found with the body of a single male, 30–35 years old, dubbed the “Griffin Warrior.” Many of the grave goods were manufactured in the Minoan world. Among the gold artifacts were four signet rings decorated with Minoan ritual scenes. Here we discuss the excavation of the grave, describe the rings, and consider the significance of the rings’ iconography for the Mycenaeans who buried them.

Key takeaways

![Image 1: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)

AI




---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  The discovery of the Griffin Warrior's grave in 2015 revealed significant Minoan artifacts, influencing Mycenaean understanding.
2.  Four gold signet rings, adorned with Minoan iconography, were found, highlighting cultural connections between Pylos and Crete.
3.  The grave dates to Late Helladic IIA, around 1450-1400 BCE, based on associated pottery and grave goods.
4.  Excavation revealed a robust male skeleton, approximately 30-35 years old, interred with extensive grave goods.
5.  The text aims to describe and analyze the significance of the gold rings and their implications for Mycenaean culture.

What new insights were revealed about the burial practices of the Griffin Warrior?addThe excavation revealed the Griffin Warrior was interred in a wooden coffin, surrounded by a wealth of grave goods, suggesting complex burial rituals typical of high-status individuals around LH IIA (ca. 1450-1400 BCE). This included no clay vessels, an unusual practice indicating a preference for metal over ceramic offerings.

How does the construction of the Griffin Warrior's grave differ from other Mycenaean graves?addThe burial chamber lacked the structural ledges typical in Mycenaean shaft graves, and its depth and construction were notably distinct from those at Mycenae. This raises questions about the evolution of funerary architecture during the Early Mycenaean period, particularly in the context of LH IIA.

What does the discovery of the gold rings suggest about Minoan influence in Mycenaean culture?addThe four gold signet rings found in the grave closely adhere to Minoan iconographic prototypes, indicating a significant cultural transmission from Crete to Pylos. Their construction techniques further suggest a Minoan origin, reinforcing the intricate relationship between these civilizations at the start of the Late Bronze Age.

How were the grave goods arranged in relation to the body of the Griffin Warrior?addThe arrangement and classification of grave goods followed a structural logic, with weapons exclusively to the left of the body while rings clustered with sealstones on the right. This indicates a nuanced understanding of the symbolic roles of these artifacts in relation to the deceased.

This aligns with the absence of later artifacts, reinforcing the proposed temporal framework for the burial context.
